newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn gold plan criticised after Buba rejection.
newsitem.headline: Bonn gold plan criticised after Buba rejection.

text.p: A German government plan to revalue its official reserves came under heavy criticism on Friday as several leading economists warned the scheme could hurt the launch of single European currency.
Horst Siebert, a member of Bonn's economic advisory council known as the "five wisemen," said the revaluation plan dampens hopes for a good start to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The whole plan is strongly impaired in its credibility and with it also the future (single) currency in its stability," Siebert told the Hamburger Abendblatt newspaper.
The Bundesbank on Wednesday rejected Bonn's plan to revalue the central bank's reserves in an effort to bolster government finances.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel suggested the revaluation more than a week ago, but the Bundesbank's opposition has unleashed a torrent of criticism in Germany and other European Union nations. The bank said the plan infringed on its independence.

Siebert said it would be "wreckless" to endanger foreign confidence in the Bundesbank, but added strong reaction against the revaluation by the public and economists could force Bonn to back away from the plan.
He also favoured a delay in EMU if the criteria laid out in the Maastricht treat cannot be met credibly.

Other criticism came from a Bundesbank member Wilhelm Noelling, who told the same Hamburg newspaper that a currency union that comes together under long foreseeable turbulence would have no chance for a confident start.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Associaion of German Industry (BDI), said the rift could have negative impact on the economy.
"Unfortunately it has come to the fatal and right impression that the efforts to plug the budget gap and achieve the Maastricht criteria have failed," he told the Neue Osnabruecker Zeitung.
The revaluation plan would only lead to gains on paper, he said, noting that companies don't revalue inventory to create profit. "You can only pay out real profit," he said.
Meanwhile, a budget expert of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats called for a final decision on a revaluation.

"I am astounded over the contradictory statements," Juergen Koppelin told the Express newspaper. A week ago "Theo Waigel said in a special meeting of the coalition that the Bundesbank would approve of this step. Now suddenly that is different."

The revaluation plan would bring the Bundesbank a windfall of 40 billion marks ($24 billion) because Germany books its gold at 144 marks per ounce while the market price is much higher at 600 marks per ounce.
Waigel suggested a revaluation after estimates indicated 1997 tax revenue would fall some 18 billion short of targets. The German budget was already under pressure from near-record unemployment.
The Maastricht treaty requires EU members joining EMU at the planned 1999 start to have budget deficits of three percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
Many economist predict Germany will miss the target, although Bonn has forecast a figure of 2.9 percent. ($ = 1.700 German Marks)
